South African police have deployed rubber bullets in Johannesburg neighborhoods in a desperate bid to halt a wave of violent attacks targeting foreign nationals. The unrest has already claimed 22 lives and forced approximately 13,000 people from their homes, marking one of the most severe outbreaks of xenophobic violence the country has experienced in recent years.

Armed with makeshift weapons including clubs, machetes, and axes, rioters have systematically targeted foreigners living in South African communities. Zimbabwean nationals have borne the brunt of this violence, many having fled to South Africa seeking refuge from the economic collapse and political repression plaguing their home country. # South African Police Fire Rubber Bullets as Xenophobic Violence Rages On

**JOHANNESBURG** — Police fired rubber bullets and used tear gas Thursday to disperse mobs in the townships surrounding Johannesburg, attempting to bring an end to a week of xenophobic violence that has left at least 22 people dead and forced more than 13,000 others to flee their homes.

The violence, which began in the impoverished settlement of Alexandra before spreading to other townships, has been marked by shocking brutality. Armed with clubs, machetes, and axes, mobs of South Africans have hunted down foreign nationals—many of them refugees and migrants from Zimbabwe, but also from Mozambique, Malawi, and other neighboring countries—dragging them from their homes, beating them, and in some cases burning them alive. Shacks and shops belonging to foreigners have been looted and torched, leaving entire blocks of the poorest neighborhoods in ruins.

Witnesses described scenes of terror as gangs moved from shack to shack, demanding identity documents and attacking anyone unable to prove South African citizenship. "They came with pangas and sticks, shouting that we must go back to our country," said one Zimbabwean man who fled with his family to a nearby police station, one of several improvised shelters now housing thousands of displaced people. Local churches have also opened their doors to those seeking safety, with community halls and school buildings pressed into service as makeshift refugee camps.

The unrest has been fueled by deep-seated frustrations among poor South Africans, who accuse foreign nationals of taking scarce jobs, driving down wages, and straining already limited housing and services. Unemployment in South Africa remains stubbornly high, particularly in townships like Alexandra, and many residents say they feel abandoned by a government that has failed to deliver on promises of jobs and housing more than a decade after the end of apartheid. Zimbabweans, in particular, have borne the brunt of the attacks; an estimated three million have crossed into South Africa in recent years, fleeing economic collapse and political repression under President Robert Mugabe.

President Thabo Mbeki condemned the violence in a nationally televised address, calling the attacks "a shocking betrayal of the values of our Constitution" and vowing that police would restore order and bring perpetrators to justice. "There can be no justification whatsoever for the violence we have seen this week," Mbeki said, urging South Africans to remember the support many African nations gave the country during its own struggle against apartheid.

The violence has drawn sharp condemnation from leaders across the continent. The African Union and several regional governments issued statements expressing alarm over the attacks, with some officials warning that the unrest threatened to tarnish South Africa's image as a haven of stability and economic opportunity in the region.

Despite the deployment of additional police units and the use of rubber bullets to break up crowds, sporadic attacks have continued to be reported in scattered pockets around Johannesburg, and there are fears the violence could spread to other cities. Human rights organizations have called for a more robust government response, warning that without decisive action, the death toll and displacement figures are likely to rise further.

For now, thousands remain crowded into shelters, uncertain when—or if—they will be able to return to homes that in many cases no longer exist.

# Johannesburg: The Heartbeat of South Africa

Johannesburg, often affectionately called "Jozi" or "Joburg," stands as South Africa's largest city and the economic powerhouse of the entire African continent. Unlike many major cities that owe their existence to rivers or coastlines, Johannesburg was born from gold—specifically, the discovery of the Witwatersrand gold reef in 1886, which sparked a rush that transformed the area from quiet farmland into a bustling metropolis within just a few years.

## A City Shaped by History

Johannesburg's history is deeply intertwined with South Africa's complex past. During the apartheid era, the city became a symbol of both oppression and resistance. Soweto, a township on Johannesburg's outskirts, played a pivotal role in the anti-apartheid movement, most notably during the 1976 student uprising that drew international attention to the injustices of the regime. Today, sites like the Apartheid Museum and Nelson Mandela's former home in Soweto serve as powerful reminders of this turbulent history and the long walk to freedom that followed.

## Economic and Cultural Hub

As South Africa's financial capital, Johannesburg hosts the Johannesburg Stock Exchange, the largest in Africa, along with numerous multinational corporations and financial institutions. The city's economy extends beyond mining into finance, manufacturing, and technology, making it a magnet for job seekers from across the continent.

Culturally, Johannesburg is incredibly diverse, reflecting South Africa's status as the "Rainbow Nation." The city is home to people from all eleven official language groups, as well as immigrants from across Africa and beyond. This diversity is evident in neighborhoods like Maboneng and Braamfontein, which have transformed into vibrant arts districts filled with galleries, street art, restaurants, and markets showcasing local creativity.

## Challenges and Resilience

Like many major cities, Johannesburg faces significant challenges, including economic inequality, crime, and infrastructure struggles. The stark contrast between affluent suburbs like Sandton—often called Africa's richest square mile—and underserved townships highlights the ongoing work needed to address South Africa's legacy of inequality.

Despite these challenges, Johannesburg's resilience shines through. The city continues to reinvent itself, with urban renewal projects breathing new life into once-neglected areas, and a thriving creative scene that includes music, fashion, and culinary innovation drawing inspiration from across Africa.

## Conclusion

Johannesburg embodies the complexities of modern South Africa—a nation grappling with its past while building toward an ambitious future. As the country's largest city, it serves as both a gateway to Africa for international business and a living testament to the resilience of its people, making it an essential destination for understanding South Africa's story.

**Wave of Xenophobic Violence Rocks Johannesburg, Leaving Dozens Dead and Thousands Displaced**

*By CNN Staff*

JOHANNESBURG, South Africa — A surge of xenophobic attacks targeting foreign nationals has swept through townships and inner-city neighborhoods in Johannesburg over the past week, leaving communities shattered, homes reduced to ashes, and a death toll that continues to climb.

According to local authorities, at least 12 people have been confirmed dead, with dozens more injured in violence that erupted in areas including Alexandra, Diepsloot, and parts of the central business district. Community leaders and aid organizations warn the actual toll may be higher, as bodies continue to be recovered from burned-out shacks and makeshift shelters.

The violence, which appears to have been triggered by rising economic tensions and false rumors blaming foreign nationals for crime and job losses, has forced an estimated 3,000 to 5,000 people—primarily from Mozambique, Zimbabwe, Malawi, and other African nations—to flee their homes. Many are now sheltering in police stations, community halls, and makeshift camps set up by humanitarian groups.

"We have lost everything. My shop was burned, my home was looted, and now we sleep on the floor of a church with nothing," said one Mozambican shopkeeper who requested anonymity for fear of further retaliation.

Videos circulating on social media show mobs looting foreign-owned businesses and setting fire to homes, while residents accuse armed groups of going door-to-door demanding identification documents. Human rights organizations have condemned the attacks as a resurgence of the deadly xenophobic violence that gripped South Africa in 2008 and again in 2019, incidents that similarly left dozens dead and thousands displaced.

**Government Response**

South African President Cyril Ramaphosa issued a statement condemning the violence, calling it "a betrayal of our constitutional values and the spirit of ubuntu that defines who we are as a nation."

"There is no justification, none whatsoever, for South Africans to attack fellow human beings because of where they were born," Ramaphosa said during a press briefing in Pretoria. He announced the deployment of additional police units to affected areas and promised a full investigation into the causes of the unrest.

Police Minister Bheki Cele confirmed that dozens of arrests have been made, though critics argue the police response has been slow and insufficient given the scale of destruction.

"We have seen this before, and each time the government promises action, yet here we are again," said Sipho Mkhize, a researcher with the African Centre for Migration and Society. "The root causes—poverty, unemployment, and inequality—are never adequately addressed."

**International and Regional Reactions**

Neighboring countries have expressed alarm over the violence. Mozambique's government summoned South Africa's ambassador to demand assurances for the safety of its citizens, while Zimbabwe's foreign ministry issued a statement urging Pretoria to "take decisive action to protect all residents regardless of nationality."

The African Union released a statement calling for calm and urging South African authorities to "swiftly bring perpetrators to justice and address the underlying socioeconomic tensions fueling xenophobic sentiment."

The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) has mobilized emergency response teams to assist displaced individuals, providing food, water, and medical care at shelter sites across the city.

**A Cycle of Violence**

Analysts point to South Africa's persistently high unemployment rate—hovering above 32%—as a key driver of tensions, with disinformation campaigns on social media further inflaming hostility toward foreign nationals, who are often scapegoated for the country's economic struggles.

Civil society groups have called for long-term solutions, including stronger law enforcement accountability, economic reforms, and public education campaigns to combat xenophobia.

As the death toll rises and displaced families remain in limbo, questions continue to mount over whether this latest eruption of violence will lead to lasting change—or simply become another chapter in a recurring and painful pattern.

*This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.*

# Xenophobic Violence Erupts Across South Africa, Sparking National Crisis

**Johannesburg, May 2008** — South Africa is grappling with a wave of deadly xenophobic violence that erupted in Alexandra Township, a densely populated settlement north of Johannesburg, before spreading rapidly to other urban centers across the country.

## Violence Begins in Alexandra

The unrest began in mid-May when residents of Alexandra Township launched attacks against foreign nationals, primarily targeting migrants and refugees from Zimbabwe, Mozambique, Malawi, and other African nations. Mobs armed with machetes, sticks, and makeshift weapons stormed homes and informal settlements, looting shops owned by foreign nationals and setting fire to shacks.

Witnesses described scenes of chaos as residents accused immigrants of taking jobs, housing, and business opportunities from South African citizens amid widespread poverty and unemployment. The violence quickly spread beyond Alexandra to other townships in Gauteng province, then to KwaZulu-Natal, the Western Cape, and beyond, leaving a trail of destruction.

## Death Toll Rises, Thousands Displaced

At least several dozen people have been killed in the violence, with hundreds more injured. Tens of thousands of foreign nationals have been displaced, seeking refuge in police stations, community halls, churches, and makeshift camps as their homes and businesses were destroyed.

## Police and Military Response

South African Police Service (SAPS) officers were deployed in large numbers to affected areas, though critics argue the initial response was slow and insufficient to contain the rapidly spreading violence. As the crisis deepened, the government took the significant step of deploying the South African National Defence Force (SANDF) to assist police in restoring order in the worst-affected townships — a rare move underscoring the severity of the crisis.

Authorities have made hundreds of arrests in connection with the attacks, looting, and related violence, though human rights groups have called for more decisive action to protect vulnerable communities.

## Mbeki Condemns the Violence

President Thabo Mbeki addressed the nation, expressing shock and condemnation over the attacks. "We will not allow that anybody should be victimized because they come from another part of our continent," Mbeki stated, describing the violence as a betrayal of South Africa's values of ubuntu and its history of receiving support from African neighbors during the anti-apartheid struggle.

Mbeki emphasized that the government would take firm action against perpetrators while working to address the underlying socioeconomic tensions fueling xenophobic sentiment, including poverty, unemployment, and competition for scarce resources in townships.

## Nelson Mandela Foundation Speaks Out

The Nelson Mandela Foundation issued a strongly worded statement condemning the violence as a betrayal of South Africa's constitutional values and its history of solidarity with the rest of Africa. The Foundation called on all South Africans to reject xenophobia and recommit to the principles of human dignity and unity enshrined in the country's post-apartheid constitution.

"Our liberation was made possible by the support and sacrifice of our brothers and sisters across this continent," the Foundation noted, urging citizens to remember the debt owed to neighboring countries that sheltered South African exiles during the apartheid era.

## Ongoing Crisis

As the violence continues to unfold, humanitarian organizations, faith-based groups, and civil society networks have mobilized to provide emergency shelter, food, and medical assistance to displaced foreign nationals. Government officials have pledged to investigate the root causes of the unrest and to hold accountable those responsible for inciting and carrying out attacks.

The crisis has drawn international attention and concern from neighboring African nations, raising urgent questions about migration policy, economic inequality, and social cohesion in post-apartheid South Africa.

*This is a developing story.*

# Fires of Fear: Xenophobic Violence Grips Johannesburg Townships

*Johannesburg — In the pre-dawn hours, smoke still curled above the tin roofs of Alexandra township, where charred remains of shops once owned by immigrant traders smoldered in the wreckage of what officials are calling one of the worst outbreaks of xenophobic violence in years.*

## A Night of Terror

The violence erupted late Tuesday when mobs armed with machetes, sticks, and makeshift torches moved through narrow township streets, targeting shops and homes belonging to foreign nationals—many from Zimbabwe, Mozambique, Malawi, and Somalia. By morning, at least a dozen shops lay in ashes, and displaced families huddled in community halls and police stations, uncertain if they had homes to return to.

"They came with fire in their hands and hate in their eyes," said Grace Moyo, a 34-year-old Zimbabwean shopkeeper who fled with her two children as her spaza shop burned. "I have lived here for six years. My children were born here. But last night, none of that mattered. We were just foreigners to them."

Moyo, like dozens of others, spent the night at a local police station, wrapped in a blanket donated by a neighbor, watching smoke rise over the neighborhood she once called home.

## Voices from the Ashes

Residents described scenes of chaos as looters stripped shops bare before setting them alight. Local shopkeeper Thabo Ndlovu, a South African who tried to shield his Ethiopian neighbor's store from looters, recounted the fear that gripped the community.

"I told them, 'This man has done nothing wrong. He sells bread to your children.' But they didn't want to hear reason. They said the foreigners are taking our jobs, our women, our future," Ndlovu said, standing amid the debris of the shop he tried to protect. "This is not who we are. This is fear turned into fire."

Community elder Nomvula Khumalo, who has lived in Alexandra for over 40 years, expressed grief over the destruction. "I remember when neighbors helped neighbors, no matter where they came from. Now I see hatred eating us alive. Where will this end?"

## Casualties and Displacement

Local hospitals confirmed at least three deaths linked to the violence, with dozens more injured, some critically, after clashes between residents and immigrant communities trying to defend their properties. The South African Red Cross estimates over 300 people have been displaced, seeking shelter in makeshift camps, churches, and police compounds.

Amara Osei, a Nigerian trader whose electronics shop was looted and burned, described the panic of fleeing with nothing but the clothes on his back. "I built that shop for ten years. Tonight, it's ash. I don't know where my family will sleep. I don't know if we are safe anywhere in this country now."

## Official Response
